summary: Specifies the DDoS Open Threat Signaling (DOTS) signal channel, a protocol a client uses to ask a mitigation server for protection against DDoS attacks. It is designed to work even under attack conditions. It was replaced by RFC 9132.

eli5.summary: When a flood of unwanted visitors arrives, you press an alarm button to call for help. This is that button for networks.

subtitle: A protocol for requesting DDoS mitigation protection over the network.

tldr.problem: When a network comes under a DDoS attack, the victim may not know exactly what is happening. They need a way to quickly signal to a mitigation service 'I am under attack, please help' even while under attack when normal communication is difficult.
tldr.mechanism: DOTS Signal Channel is a lightweight protocol built on CoAP (Constrained Application Protocol) that allows a client to request DDoS mitigation from a server. The client sends mitigation requests specifying the target IP addresses, ports, or domain names under attack, and the server responds with the status of the mitigation. The protocol operates over both UDP (with DTLS encryption) and TCP (with TLS encryption) to ensure reliability even during attacks.
tldr.outcome: The specification was replaced by RFC 9132 with an updated version. DOTS enables automated, coordinated DDoS defense across administrative boundaries.

facts.label: Encryption
facts.value: DTLS over UDP or TLS over TCP

today: RFC 9132 is the current specification for the DOTS Signal Channel, replacing this version with updates and clarifications. DOTS is deployed in DDoS mitigation services and customer equipment for coordinated attack defense.

sections.title: The DDoS Problem and DOTS
sections.content:
A Distributed Denial-of-Service attack is an attempt to make a network resource unavailable by overwhelming it with traffic from many sources. Attackers might flood a server with TCP SYN packets (memory exhaustion), send ACK floods (CPU exhaustion), or simply send more traffic than the link can carry (bandwidth exhaustion). The victim may not know what is happening or how to stop it. DOTS (Distributed Denial-of-Service Open Threat Signaling) is a protocol that allows a DOTS client (the victim) to signal a DOTS server (a mitigation service) requesting protection against detected, suspected, or anticipated attacks. This document specifies the DOTS Signal Channel, a lightweight, reliable communication mechanism for this signaling.

In typical deployments, the DOTS client is a router or firewall protecting a customer's network, while the DOTS server is operated by a DDoS mitigation service provider. The two are in different administrative domains. The DOTS server works with a mitigator to enable traffic filtering on behalf of the client, and communicates back the status of mitigation efforts.
sections.eli5: You tell a DDoS protection company 'I am under attack on server 192.0.2.1' and they use their big network to filter out the bad traffic before it reaches you. DOTS is how you make that request.

sections.title: Design and Protocol Stack
sections.content:
The DOTS Signal Channel is built on top of the Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP), a lightweight protocol originally designed for devices with limited resources. CoAP provides the request-response mechanism, congestion control, and small message overhead needed for signaling during attacks when network conditions are poor and packet loss is expected. The signal channel uses CoAP over either DTLS (Datagram TLS) on UDP or TLS on TCP, chosen for their ability to work reliably even when network conditions degrade. The choice of both UDP and TCP, called 'Happy Eyeballs', allows the client to quickly fall back to TCP if the UDP path is blocked by a middlebox.

Messages are serialized using CBOR (Concise Binary Object Representation), a compact binary encoding that keeps message sizes small to avoid fragmentation. The entire stack is managed by YANG data models, which specify the structure of mitigation requests and responses in a protocol-independent way.

DOTS clients and servers use port 4646 by default. Once a signal channel is established, DOTS agents may periodically send heartbeat messages to keep the channel active. If the signal channel goes silent, the server can trigger preconfigured mitigation for that client.
sections.eli5: Think of the stack like a postal service: DOTS is the form you fill out, CoAP is the mechanism for getting that form delivered reliably, CBOR is the compression to make the form smaller, and DTLS/TLS is the secure envelope. Port 4646 is the mailbox.

sections.title: Requesting Mitigation
sections.content:
When a DOTS client detects an attack, it sends a PUT request to the DOTS server specifying the mitigation scope: which IP addresses, prefixes, port ranges, domain names, or URIs are under attack. The client must include a lifetime (how long the mitigation should stay active) and can include additional attack details. Each mitigation request is assigned a unique identifier ('mid', mitigation ID) and the client is identified by a 'cuid' (Client Unique Identifier), typically derived from a hash of the client's certificate or pre-shared key.

The server responds with a 2.xx success code if the mitigation request is accepted, or an error code if something is wrong. While mitigation is active, the server periodically sends status messages with details about the attack and the effectiveness of the mitigation. The client can update the attack information with efficacy updates or withdraw the mitigation request entirely by sending a DELETE.

To avoid conflicts when multiple DOTS clients in the same domain send overlapping mitigation requests, the server detects conflicts and notifies clients, allowing them to adjust their requests. The protocol uses CoAP Non-confirmable messages for request/response exchanges to minimize overhead during attacks.
sections.eli5: You send a message saying 'Mitigate attacks on 192.0.2.0/24 on port 443 for 1 hour' and the server replies 'OK, we are filtering that now.' While the mitigation is active, the server sends updates like 'We blocked 10 million packets in the last minute.'

sections.title: Session Configuration and Heartbeat
sections.content:
Before sending mitigation requests, DOTS clients and servers can negotiate configuration parameters for the signal channel session. The client sends a PUT request to the /config URI path, specifying parameters such as the heartbeat interval (how often to send keepalives) and the session lifetime. This allows both sides to agree on how frequently heartbeats will be sent and when the session expires if inactive.

Heartbeats are simple GET requests sent periodically by both the client and server to keep the signal channel active. If a heartbeat is not received within the expected interval, the other side assumes the channel has failed. If configured, this channel loss can automatically trigger preconfigured mitigation requests, allowing the client to 'arm' mitigation to activate if the control connection fails.

Redirected signaling is also supported: a DOTS server can redirect a client to a different server address, allowing load balancing and failover.
sections.eli5: Before asking for help, you agree with the service 'I will check in every 30 seconds so you know I am still there. If you do not hear from me, trigger the prepared mitigation plan.' This is like a dead-man's switch for DDoS protection.

sections.title: Happy Eyeballs and Message Exchange
sections.content:
To avoid long connection setup delays during attacks, DOTS uses a 'Happy Eyeballs' procedure similar to the one in IPv6 connection establishment. The client attempts to connect to the DOTS server using both IPv6 and IPv4, and tries both DTLS over UDP and TLS over TCP in parallel, with a short delay between attempts. The client uses whichever connection succeeds first, caching the result to avoid repeated attempts. If the TLS over TCP connection succeeds when DTLS failed, the client will periodically retry DTLS to see if the UDP path becomes available.

DOTS agents must respect rate-limiting rules: they send at most one UDP datagram per round-trip time on average. If the client cannot estimate RTT, it limits itself to one Non-confirmable request every 3 seconds. Requests must not be delayed by congestion control checks, ensuring mitigation requests are delivered promptly even during severe attacks.

The signal channel uses CoAP methods: PUT to request or update mitigation, GET to retrieve status or subscribe to notifications, and DELETE to withdraw mitigation. All messages are marked Non-confirmable to minimize overhead during attacks while being sent repeatedly until a response is received.
sections.eli5: The client tries UDP-over-IPv6, then UDP-over-IPv4, then TCP-over-IPv6, then TCP-over-IPv4 all at once (with short delays). Whichever works first is used. This prevents the client from getting stuck waiting for a broken path to time out.

messages.label: PUT /mitigate (target-prefix, lifetime)
messages.note: Client requests mitigation for attack target.

messages.label: Periodic Status Updates
messages.note: Server sends attack status and mitigation effectiveness.

messages.label: DELETE /mitigate (mid)
messages.note: Client withdraws mitigation when attack ends.
